<a id="entry-automate-division-ontology-catalog-sync-with-trusted-merge-policy"></a>

## Entry 1 — 2026-09-26 — Automate division ontology catalog sync with trusted merge policy

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The division catalog currently lives in one repository and needs to collect all concepts from approved related repositories. Routine source changes should arrive without repeated human instructions, while division stewards retain authority over shared meaning, links and source registration.

## Decision

Run a 30-minute and manual sync in division-ontology, using scoped GitHub App installation tokens to read sources and update a fixed catalog PR. Verify generated output from trusted default-branch code before an automatic merge. Require a current division steward approval for authored changes and linked-concept drift. Poll review decisions from the default branch and retrigger the trusted gate. Keep source onboarding and generated output in separate PRs.

## Consequences

After the one-time App and branch-rule setup, unchanged or unlinked source updates require no human action. A new private source still needs steward approval and addition to the App installation. Linked-concept changes wait for a current steward decision. Scheduled runs can fail visibly when a source is inaccessible or malformed, leaving the published catalog intact. The App has latent write permission on all installed repositories; the setup guide documents a two-App alternative.

<a id="entry-docs-accept-one-action-source-onboarding-vision"></a>

## Entry 2 — 2026-11-02 — docs: accept one-action source onboarding vision

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

An approved source repository owner currently needs several coordinated steps to join the division catalog despite having administration access to their own repository. The owner has no write access to division-ontology, and the product goal is to remove a separate registration action.

## Decision

The source owner's enrollment action will be granting a preapproved, selected-repository, read-only GitHub App access to their repository. A valid source should appear after normal sync, with all committed concepts imported and clear status for attempts, publication, failures, and revoked access. Cross-source equivalence and shared-term governance remain separate.

## Consequences

The analyst must define discovery, validation, publication, failure isolation, status, and revocation behavior consistent with one owner action. The architect must design a genuinely read-only source access path and preserve catalog provenance. This vision does not choose the implementation mechanism.

<a id="entry-policy-add-alternate-steward-code-owner"></a>

## Entry 3 — 2026-11-02 — policy: add alternate steward code owner

*Kind: governance. Status: accepted.*

## Context

PR #21 exposed a review deadlock: the trusted policy recognized only `@jamiemitchellconsultants`, which had authored the PR and could not approve its own work. An alternate account with write access is available for review.

## Decision

List `@james-mitchell-ba` as a code owner for the existing sensitive paths and recognize current-head approval from either `@jamiemitchellconsultants` or `@james-mitchell-ba` in `merge-policy`. An unresolved changes request by either steward continues to block the check.

## Consequences

Future authored and linked-concept changes can pass the trusted policy after approval by either listed steward account at the current head. CODEOWNERS review requests remain advisory to the required `merge-policy` check.

## Entry 4 — 2026-11-04 — Define runtime knowledge workspace vision

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

<a id="entry-define-runtime-knowledge-workspace-behaviours"></a>

## Entry 5 — 2026-11-04 — Define runtime knowledge workspace behaviours

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

Feature #25 combines a published knowledge baseline with persistent human-authored context and relationships. Its accepted vision left snapshot changes, contribution ownership, history, simultaneous edits, optional codification and missing JWT roles to analysis. These need precise observable outcomes before architecture can proceed.

## Decision

Retain contributions when endpoints disappear, mark them unavailable and exclude their relationships from default traversal while allowing explicit inclusion. Any ManageKnowledgeGraph user may edit or remove contributions, with preserved history and explicit review of stale edits. Contributors may choose published relationship types or supply custom meanings. Codification associations are explicit and preserve both provenances. Access requires a valid JWT with a workspace role; no-role tokens receive no implicit reader access.

Add PublishedKnowledgeSnapshot, KnowledgeAnnotation, RuntimeRelationship, KnowledgeContributionChange and CodificationAssociation with definitions sourced from the accepted vision and analyst decisions. Existing term IRIs, StaffId meaning, source registrations and reviewed links are preserved.

## Consequences

Architecture can work from the accepted behaviours once this PR is reviewed and merged. The external InternalOntology/C4 graph contracts and identifiers must be confirmed before implementation planning; pilot product, owner, wider-business reviewer and representative search examples are deferred to acceptance planning. The new shared terms require division-steward approval.

Generated catalog outputs were built, checked and reviewed locally. They are excluded from this authored PR; scheduled sync will propose the generated-only update after merge.

## Entry 6 — 2026-11-04 — Narrow merge policy to ontology imports

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The existing gate is broader than needed for external ontology imports and blocks unrelated changes. The main branch ruleset has no blanket required approval or required code-owner approval.

## Decision

Require the check's current steward approval for source registration changes and linked-concept drift. Verified routine refreshes pass automatically; other changes pass the check.

## Consequences

Changes to trusted policy and workflow files also pass this check without steward approval. CODEOWNERS still requests reviews, and repository governance continues to call for applicable reviews, but the ruleset does not enforce those approvals. Incomplete pull-request file lists fail closed.

<a id="entry-define-c4-impact-assessment-vision"></a>

## Entry 7 — 2026-11-04 — Define C4 impact assessment vision

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

Architects need to assess change impact across systems and repositories. The division catalogue records source concepts and commits but does not yet turn architecture facts into C4 views. InternalOntology now publishes a versioned source knowledge graph with evidence and coverage; no participating repository must provide every C4 level. The product owner asked for architects as the first users and for a pilot that permits subjective feedback.

## Decision

Adopt a vision in which architects use source-backed C4 views to make and explain impact assessments. Support system context, container, component and code views when evidence exists, preserve provenance and uncertainty, and accept partial coverage without blocking source admission. Evaluate the first pilot through structured architect and reviewer feedback on perceived accuracy, completeness, suspected misses, false leads and confidence.

## Consequences

The analyst can define the user-visible impact-assessment behaviours and coverage states after this PR merges. The first pilot has no independently adjudicated reference set or zero-miss threshold. Graph authoring remains in source repositories; renderer, interaction design and detailed source contract remain open for later phases.

<a id="entry-define-c4-impact-assessment-behaviours"></a>

## Entry 8 — 2026-11-04 — Define C4 impact assessment behaviours

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The accepted vision calls for architects to assess change requests across participating repositories using all four C4 levels where source evidence permits. The upstream source graph distinguishes assertions, evidence, inferences, commits and coverage. The analyst phase needed precise rules for starting from a request, following possible impacts, showing partial views, and avoiding false assurance when facts are missing.

## Decision

Accept the 15 observable behaviours in `02-behaviours.md`. An architect may start with a change request description alone, confirm candidate elements, follow only evidenced relationship steps, and produce a human-reviewed ImpactAssessment. Context diagrams may show an evidenced external system whose repository has not joined, without presenting that repository as a participating source. C4Diagram and ImpactAssessment become division shared terms; existing source identities and equivalence governance remain intact.

## Consequences

The architect phase must choose the graph-to-C4 mapping, rendering and assessment output mechanism while preserving the specified evidence, snapshot and gap behaviours. Missing C4 levels remain visible and do not block source admission. The first pilot uses subjective architect and reviewer feedback without a numeric accuracy gate. The core term additions require division-steward review; generated catalogue changes follow in a separate sync PR.

<a id="entry-define-c4-impact-assessment-architecture"></a>

## Entry 9 — 2026-11-04 — Define C4 impact assessment architecture

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The accepted [C4 impact behaviours](https://github.com/jamiemitchellconsultants/division-ontology/pull/41) require evidence-backed paths across participating repositories, four C4 levels where source facts permit, reproducible source revisions, and explicit gaps. The current catalog publishes ontology concepts and source commits but does not hold source graph instances or assessments. The first pilot needs an architecture that can be evaluated before a hosted workspace is chosen.

## Decision

Accept the [architecture](https://github.com/jamiemitchellconsultants/division-ontology/blob/feature/c4-diagrams-from-source-knowledge-graphs/architect/docs/features/c4-diagrams-from-source-knowledge-graphs/03-architecture.md): a local Node.js CLI reads source graphs at the published catalog's pinned commits and creates deterministic JSON and Markdown/Mermaid views plus architect-authored, reviewable assessments. Reviewed C4 mappings determine levels and boundaries; reviewed cross-source bindings connect an evidenced external node to a participating source node without merging source identities. These decisions are recorded in [ADR 0001](https://github.com/jamiemitchellconsultants/division-ontology/blob/feature/c4-diagrams-from-source-knowledge-graphs/architect/docs/adr/0001-local-pinned-c4-pilot.md), [ADR 0002](https://github.com/jamiemitchellconsultants/division-ontology/blob/feature/c4-diagrams-from-source-knowledge-graphs/architect/docs/adr/0002-reviewed-c4-mappings.md), and [ADR 0003](https://github.com/jamiemitchellconsultants/division-ontology/blob/feature/c4-diagrams-from-source-knowledge-graphs/architect/docs/adr/0003-reviewed-cross-source-bindings.md).

## Consequences

The developer plan can use the existing catalog as the source inventory and revision lock while keeping graph facts source-owned and authored mappings separate from generated outputs. Missing graphs, unresolved mappings and absent relationships appear as gaps, not evidence of no impact. JointBooking currently has no source graph in its checkout, so source-backed C4 pilot paths remain unavailable until it publishes one. The local pilot requires read access to the participating source commits; a later workspace can consume the same view model.

<a id="entry-plan-c4-impact-assessment-pilot"></a>

## Entry 11 — 2026-11-04 — Plan C4 impact assessment pilot

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The accepted C4 impact assessment vision, B1–B15 behaviours, architecture and ADRs call for a local, pinned-source pilot with evidence-backed views and architect-authored assessments. The developer needs an independently reviewable build sequence before code is written. The current catalog contains JointBooking, whose pinned source checkout has no source graph.

## Decision

Plan the pilot as ten test-first tasks: pinned catalog and source loading, source graph and coverage parsing, reviewed C4 mappings and cross-source bindings, candidate search, directed impact paths, four-level projection, pinned code inspection, deterministic rendering, editable assessments and qualitative feedback, then CLI integration. The detailed plan fixes interfaces, schemas, fixture data, tests and a commit and push for each task. Synthetic two-source fixtures prove cross-source and four-level behaviour without inventing JointBooking facts.

## Consequences

The build phase can implement the accepted architecture in small reviewable commits after this plan is reviewed and merged. Missing source graphs and stale references remain visible gaps. Real JointBooking C4 paths depend on upstream source graph adoption. This PR changes only authored plans; generated dist/ remains separate.

<a id="entry-build-c4-impact-assessment-pilot"></a>

## Entry 12 — 2026-11-04 — Build C4 impact assessment pilot

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

Architects need a reproducible way to investigate change-request impacts across participating repositories while retaining source ownership, evidence and unknown coverage. The accepted C4 architecture and merged developer plan define a local pilot over pinned catalog and source commits.

## Decision

Implement the local C4 pilot: pinned snapshot and graph readers, reviewed mapping and binding registries, candidate search, directed paths, four-level projections, inspected-code evidence, deterministic reports, and editable assessment and feedback records. Empty production registries avoid inventing mappings. Coverage gaps and separate source identities remain visible, and code-view citations are revalidated against the recorded snapshot.

## Consequences

Architects can review evidence and record their own conclusions without an approval command. Source graphs remain optional and source-owned; JointBooking cannot supply graph-backed C4 paths until its source publishes a graph at a catalog-pinned revision. Generated catalog files are unchanged.

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

The pilot needed repeatable acceptance evidence for cross-system paths, pinned source evidence, incomplete coverage and assessment reporting. The original checklist called for manual output comparisons and a separate deployed run. The pilot runs as a CLI on a Mac with disposable sources.

<a id="entry-define-runtime-knowledge-workspace-architecture"></a>

## Entry 14 — 2026-11-07 — Define runtime knowledge workspace architecture

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The workspace combines a baseline published from pinned source repositories with persistent runtime contributions. It needs reproducible graph imports, immediate traversal after a contribution is saved, and the same application contract on Mac, the home lab and AWS.

- [ADR 0004](https://github.com/jamiemitchellconsultants/division-ontology/blob/b2e8ed75d151865ebaa2e608bc85f0abdb97e82e/docs/adr/0004-import-and-activate-pinned-knowledge-snapshots.md) packages pinned source artefacts and activates a validated baseline atomically.

## Entry 27 — 2026-11-10 — docs(feature): define one-action source onboarding architecture

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The accepted behaviours need a source owner's one action to join a division catalog without write access or steward approval. The current sync App has write permission across its installation, so granting it would not be read-only. Source registration changes force steward review, one invalid source fails the whole build, and `dist/` is only a function of live sources, so an earlier valid version cannot be kept when a source turns invalid or loses access. The Analyst left open how grants are discovered (U11) and which file configures an import (U10).

## Decision

Each division has a dedicated read-only source App (Contents and Metadata read) that owners add repositories to, separate from the division-writer App. Grants are found by polling the installation during the normal sync; no webhook receiver is built (ADR 0009). A source declares its ontology path and namespace in `.division-ontology.json` on its default branch, rather than overloading InternalOntology's `ontology.config.json`, whose `ontologyPath` names the Markdown view (ADR 0010). Import status is generated into `dist/` with no timestamps, and the committed `dist/` is a build input so the last valid version is carried forward. Content failures become status, while GitHub or network failures fail the run (ADR 0011). Each source records its origin; granted-source failures are isolated while registered sources stay strict; namespace conflicts favour the existing holder; and refreshes touching only granted sources classify as automatic (ADR 0012).

## Consequences

Divisions need two Apps and two sets of credentials, and a new grant can take up to two hours to appear. Granted sources can publish their own definitions in their own namespace without review, limited by the namespace checks and by links staying steward-only. `verifyRefresh` must include the base `dist/`, and readers of `catalog.sources` such as the C4 loader and the workspace importer will see granted and stale sources. The developer must confirm how to read the installation's `repository_selection` and the Contents API volume. Offering to write `.division-ontology.json` in InternalOntology's installer is a separate change in that repository.

Joining a division catalog needed a steward-approved `sources.json` change and an App with write access across its installation. ## Entry 33 — 2026-11-10 — docs(feature): one-action source onboarding acceptance

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The build passes its own tests, but its GitHub client has only run against stubs, and the behaviours are only accepted when someone follows each one from outside and the same scenarios pass as executable tests, locally and in a real division with its own pair of Apps.

## Decision

Two acceptance layers per behaviour. Locally, a scripted harness creates two divisions with the real `init-division`, five local Git repositories and a file-backed stand-in for the App installation. The same actions drive both the numbered walkthrough and the ordered executable story in `test/acceptance/onboarding.test.mjs` (B1–B17). One extra check runs the real GitHub client over HTTP against a local API stand-in. In the deployed environment, `test/acceptance/onboarding-deployed.mjs` reads the published catalog and the live source heads and reports each discrepancy; granting and committing stay manual GitHub actions. At the participant's direction the commands compare actual with expected results themselves and stop only on an exception. Locally, `npm run --silent acceptance:onboarding` lists every check by name and prints one PASS line, or the expected and actual values of a failing check. Deployed, `onboarding-deployed.mjs run` commits to the test repositories and changes the App's repository list through `gh`, dispatches the division's sync, waits for it and its refresh PR, compares the published catalog with the live repositories, and stops at the first exception; `--dry-run` lists what it would do without calling GitHub. The deployed run has not been run against GitHub. The existing `rerun.mjs` takes a suite name, so `npm run acceptance:onboarding` mirrors `acceptance:c4`.

## Consequences

Nothing changes in the product in this PR. All six criteria on #14 are ticked. Organisation policy for adding the App (U12) is out of scope for this acceptance because it runs on a personal account; it is recorded as not tested. B4 needs a second division copy. There is no supported way to remove a granted source that has lost access; it stays in the catalog marked stale. That is recorded as a known limit, not fixed here.

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The template has no registered sources and no working sync App. Its `dist/`-only PRs failed `merge-policy` at "Create source-read token" with `Integration not found`, before the policy ran, so PR #100 needed an administrator override. The fresh build in that case reads no source repository, so the token served no purpose.

Skip the source-read token when a generated refresh has nothing to read: no registered sources and no source-read App configured. The policy still verifies the candidate `dist/` against a fresh build from trusted default-branch code. Template `dist/`-only PRs can pass `merge-policy` without an App or an admin override. <a id="entry-docs-design-for-workspace-api-openapi-docs-105"></a>

## Entry 35 — 2026-11-19 — docs: design for workspace API OpenAPI docs (#105)

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

A deployed runtime knowledge workspace exposes a JSON API under `/api`, but nothing describes it except the C# routes and contract types. Integrators of other division systems, the template's own developers, and reviewers of API changes all need an accurate, always current contract, and a page where they can browse it and try calls with their own roles. Research showed that .NET 10 can generate the spec at build time, that Swagger UI supports PKCE sign-in with Keycloak and Entra, and that all three deployments already route `/api/*` to the API.

## Decision

- Generate an OpenAPI 3.1 spec from the code with `Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi`. Write a deployment-neutral copy to `runtime/openapi/workspace-api.json` on every build, commit it in the same PR as the code that changes it, and fail a new `api-contract` CI job when it is out of date ([ADR 0013](https://github.com/jamiemitchellconsultants/division-ontology/blob/feature/workspace-api-openapi-docs/design/docs/adr/0013-generate-workspace-api-spec-at-build-time.md)).
- Serve the spec at `/api/openapi/v1.json` and Swagger UI at `/api/docs` from the API, both open to anonymous visitors. Every data route keeps its existing authorisation, and no routing changes are needed ([ADR 0014](https://github.com/jamiemitchellconsultants/division-ontology/blob/feature/workspace-api-openapi-docs/design/docs/adr/0014-serve-spec-and-swagger-ui-from-the-api.md)). Scalar was considered and not chosen.
- Sign in from the docs UI with PKCE, reusing the web UI's public client in Keycloak and Entra plus one extra redirect URI. Add sign-in endpoints from the provider's discovery document only to the served spec ([ADR 0015](https://github.com/jamiemitchellconsultants/division-ontology/blob/feature/workspace-api-openapi-docs/design/docs/adr/0015-docs-ui-sign-in-reuses-web-client.md)). A separate docs client was rejected for now: it would give separate revocation and logging, but the docs UI grants nothing beyond the user's roles, and switching later needs configuration only.
- Enforce completeness with a Docker-free static test in CI, plus a hook in the existing scenario tests that fails on any observed status the spec does not declare ([ADR 0016](https://github.com/jamiemitchellconsultants/division-ontology/blob/feature/workspace-api-openapi-docs/design/docs/adr/0016-check-spec-completeness-statically-and-by-observation.md)).

## Consequences

- API contract changes become reviewable diffs, and an unregenerated change cannot pass CI.
- API startup must stay lazy, because the build-time writer runs the entry point with no database or identity configuration.
- Each identity provider needs one extra redirect URI on the existing SPA client. The API gains the `Workspace:Docs:ClientId` and `Workspace:Docs:Scopes` settings.
- The observation check only runs where the Docker-backed scenario suites run, and CI does not run those yet.
- Deliberately open: service clients for other systems, an MCP server, client SDKs, an API versioning policy, and a switch to hide the docs per deployment.

<a id="entry-docs-amend-105-design-for-refusal-bodies-and-no-server-address"></a>

## Entry 36 — 2026-11-19 — docs: amend #105 design for refusal bodies and no server address

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

While planning #105, the developer ran the workspace API from a scratch copy and found two things the accepted design (#106) got wrong.

- **Server address.** The served spec was to use the request's origin as its server address, and ASP.NET Core already does this from the Host header. In AWS, CloudFront's `AllViewerExceptHostHeader` policy gives the API the API Gateway host. In the home lab, TLS ends at Caddy, so the API sees `http://`. Swagger UI's calls would then be blocked, so readers and contributors could not try the API outside the local stack.
- **Error responses.** B2 described every error as problem details with a `code`. In fact 401, 403 and the binding failure's 400 have empty bodies, and 400 was not listed at all.

Swagger UI sends the signed-in user's token to whatever server the spec names. The API's only trust decision is JWT validation: it checks no Host, Origin or IP, and has no CORS.

## Decision

- **The vision allows one behaviour change.** The API's 400, 401 and 403 responses become problem details with fixed codes and titles: `unreadableRequest`, `authenticationRequired` and `roleRequired`. Every error therefore has one documented shape. No request changes status, and a 401 never says why a token was rejected (B22).
- **No server address in the served spec** ([ADR 0017](https://github.com/jamiemitchellconsultants/division-ontology/blob/feature/workspace-api-openapi-docs/design-amend/docs/adr/0017-serve-the-spec-without-a-server-address.md), amending ADR 0015). The framework's request-derived `servers` entry is removed, so OpenAPI's default `/` makes Swagger UI call the origin that served the docs. A spike in the browser confirmed it. Two alternatives were rejected:
  - Trusting forwarded headers would let a caller name their own host, and put users' tokens at risk if a cache or CORS rule were ever added.
  - A configured public origin is one more value that every deployment and division copy must get right.
- **One status-code hook writes the refusal bodies** ([ADR 0018](https://github.com/jamiemitchellconsultants/division-ontology/blob/feature/workspace-api-openapi-docs/design-amend/docs/adr/0018-give-refusals-fixed-problem-details-bodies.md), amending ADR 0016). A `UseStatusCodePages` hook in `ApiProgram.Configure` gives bodiless 400, 401 and 403 responses their fixed bodies, in both the container host and Lambda, with the codes kept in `ProblemResponses`. Per-event JwtBearer hooks plus `ThrowOnBadRequest` were rejected, because they would need three mechanisms for one rule. Responses given before any operation is chosen are not operation statuses, and the spec states each operation's method, path and media type instead: 404 for an unknown path, 405, 413 and 415.
- **Behaviours follow.** B2 and B3 add 400. B12, B13 and B19 name the codes. B14 and B20 drop the server address. B22 is new, and U15–U17 record the decisions.

## Consequences

- The docs UI works in all three deployments with no routing, Terraform, proxy or new setting, and nothing in a request can change where it sends a token.
- Integrators get one error shape. The Blazor web UI needs no code change, though for 403 and 400 it now shows the API's title instead of "Workspace request failed (403)." (U15).
- The served spec is the committed contract plus `workspaceSignIn` only. Offline readers of the committed file see no server address.
- A missing, invalid or expired token gets the same 401 body; only the per-request `traceId` differs.
- The draft developer plan on `feature/workspace-api-openapi-docs/plan` has sections marked pending these decisions. They are regenerated after this PR merges, before the plan PR opens.

## Entry 37 — 2026-11-19 — docs: developer plan for #105 workspace API OpenAPI docs

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The accepted design (#106, amended by #108) left the developer some open questions. A throwaway copy of `runtime/` answered each one, using SDK 10.0.302 and the pinned packages:

- **The build-time writer.** `Microsoft.Extensions.ApiDescription.Server` runs `ApiProgram.Main` inside `GetDocument.Insider` with no configuration. `ValidateOnStart` on `JwtBearerOptions` then fails the build. Nothing else resolves eagerly.
- **Determinism.** Two builds, and a build with deployment-shaped `Workspace__*` variables, produced byte-identical files.
- **Discovery.** An issuer that never replied still let the spec serve in 2.0–2.2 s, without sign-in.
- **Image publish.** `-p:OpenApiGenerateDocuments=false` turns generation off in `dotnet publish`.
- **Packages.** `Swashbuckle.AspNetCore.SwaggerUI` 10.3.1 targets net10.0 with no dependencies, and locked restore passes under Central Package Management.
- **Swagger UI sign-in.** Its PKCE redirect resolves from `window.location`, and its `/api/docs` redirect is relative.

The same work found the two problems that #108 then fixed in the design: the request-derived `servers` entry, and the empty 400, 401 and 403 bodies.

## Decision

- **Refusal responses come first (Task 2).**
  - `ProblemResponses.Refusals` holds the B22 codes and titles.
  - `UseRefusalResponses()`, a `UseStatusCodePages` hook placed straight after `UseExceptionHandler`, writes them for bodiless 400, 401 and 403 responses.
  - Doing this before the spec describes those responses means no commit describes a body that does not exist.
- **Error copy lives in one place.**
  - The spec's `unauthorized`, `forbidden` and `unreadableRequest` components are `WorkspaceProblem` responses, built from `Refusals`.
  - `ProducesWorkspaceErrors` rejects refusal codes, because `StatusFor` would describe an unknown code as 422.
- **Only `DocsSignIn` touches the served spec.** It removes `servers` unconditionally (ADR 0017), and then adds `workspaceSignIn` when it is configured. The served-spec check strips sign-in only, so any `servers` entry fails it.
- **Pre-operation statuses are left alone.**
  - The tests pin 415, 405 and 404 as empty.
  - The conformance recorder ignores 405, 413 and 415. 413 is raised while a selected endpoint reads its body, so B2 needs this to hold.
- **The tests run as Production.** `OpenApiHost` runs the API with `UseEnvironment("Production")`, as every deployment does. In Development, minimal APIs turn binding failures into 500s. API code is unchanged.
- **The architect's challenged assumption holds.** `UseStatusCodePages` only acts on a response that has not started and has no body or content type. The docs UI never returns 400, 401 or 403, and Task 8 pins that.

## Consequences

- No existing test asserts an empty 400, 401 or 403 body.
  - Task 2 extends `IdentityTests` (Keycloak and Entra), `AwsSimulationTests` (Lambda) and `WorkspaceUiTests` (U15) to check the new codes.
  - The web UI needs no code change.
- `verify-docs.sh` checks, in each deployment, that the served spec has no `servers` entry and that an anonymous data call gets `authenticationRequired`.
- The live Entra sign-in cannot be tested in this repository. It stays in the user's AWS acceptance walkthrough.
- The build starts on `feature/workspace-api-openapi-docs/build` only after this PR merges.

<a id="entry-feat-agent-friendly-openapi-decorators-and-hateoas-for-the-workspace-api"></a>

## Entry 39 — 2026-11-21 — feat: agent-friendly OpenAPI decorators and HATEOAS for the workspace API

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The workspace API's generated OpenAPI spec described routes, roles (`x-workspace-role`) and error codes (`x-workspace-codes`), but gave an agent or tool-calling client no stable tool names, no indication of which operations are safe to retry, and no discoverable path from one operation to the next. Clients had to construct follow-on URLs themselves and guess at idempotency — the POST-shaped read queries (search, traverse, entity/relationship detail) are particularly ambiguous. The HTTP `QUERY` method (RFC 10008) was evaluated as a more semantic alternative for those reads.

## Decision

Decorate every operation in the generator with a stable `operationId`, `x-agent-tool-name`, `x-agent-idempotent`, `x-agent-retryable`, `x-agent-side-effects` and input/output schema names; publish HATEOAS as OpenAPI `links` on every success response and as RFC 8288 `Link` headers at runtime, so the spec and the live service tell the same story. The completeness checker now enforces these decorators, so a future undecorated operation fails CI. The `QUERY` verb was rejected for the read queries: although .NET 10 supports it end-to-end (verified locally), API Gateway offers no native `QUERY` method, its `ANY` route is not a reliable pass-through, and this deployment's CloudFront `allowed_methods` list would reject `QUERY` before the gateway.

## Consequences

Agents can enumerate the API as 13 stable tools, decide retries from the declared flags, and follow links instead of constructing URLs; the Blazor UI is unaffected because routes, bodies and status codes did not change. The trade-off is a larger spec and a generator table that must be kept in step with new routes — mitigated by the completeness check failing undecorated operations. Deliberately open: adopting `QUERY` if API Gateway and CloudFront add native support, and any client (including the UI) choosing to consume `Link` headers instead of constructing URLs.

Re-review fixes (third commit): the `removeContribution` description now separates 409 `versionConflict` (inspect `current.removed` and review the current record, which may be another caller's edit to a still-active contribution) from 404 `contributionNotFound` (do not retry); workspace link relations moved from the unregistered URN namespace to absolute HTTPS identifiers under the project-controlled `https://github.com/jamiemitchellconsultants/division-ontology#link-relations/` namespace across runtime headers, `x-agent-discovery.linkRelations`, and the tests (the deployment-neutrality test now allows that one project namespace).

## Entry 40 — 2026-11-21 — docs: vision for traversal cursor pagination (#120)

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

`POST /api/traverse` stops at 100 paths and reports `truncated` with no way to continue, so well-connected entities — and workspace-authored relationships beyond that boundary — are unreachable through the API. The product owner accepted a vision on 21 November 2026 to make the 100-path limit a page boundary with trustworthy continuation, without disturbing existing first-page clients.

## Decision

Adopt cursor pagination for traversal as a product capability: an opaque `nextCursor`, a HATEOAS `next` link whenever another page exists, pages that carry their own entity context, and cursors bound to the original traversal parameters and a consistent snapshot/workspace view, with a clear restart-from-page-one error when that view can no longer be continued. Alternatives considered and set aside at vision level: raising or removing the 100-path limit (unbounded responses for busy nodes), and leaving truncation as-is (busy nodes stay partially invisible). Graph UI work and any change to traversal semantics stay out of scope.

## Consequences

The analyst phase inherits five measurable outcomes — every path reachable exactly once across pages, first-page compatibility, self-contained pages, trustworthy continuation with defined cursor failures, and spec-documented paging — and must turn them into behaviours, including the multi-hop frontier and cursor-invalidation cases. The architecture phase will need to decide how continuation resumes a bounded breadth-first walk without unbounded server state. Nothing about how users edit workspace data changes, and Turtle files remain read-only inputs.

## Entry 41 — 2026-11-21 — docs: behaviours for traversal cursor pagination (#121)

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The accepted vision (PR #126) left the observable behaviour of paged traversal unspecified: how continuation behaves at a multi-hop branch boundary, what a cursor binds, how each cursor failure presents, and how the bounded-work outcome would ever be measured. Without those behaviours, the architecture phase would have had to invent product semantics while designing the mechanism.

## Decision

Fix the behaviours before the mechanism. Continuation preserves today's breadth-first path order with a fixed 100-path page; `truncated` means "another page exists" on every page; each page carries its own endpoints' entity context; the runtime `next` link names `POST /api/traverse` while the cursor travels in the response body's `nextCursor`. Bounded work is specified as countable fixture measures (relationships examined per page, independent of page number and of filtered-out unavailable relationships), not as an implementation prescription. The frontier-resumption mechanism is explicitly deferred to the architect (U6), constrained by B2, B12, B16 and B17.

## Consequences

The architect inherits precise constraints: a cursor bound to parameters, snapshot and journal position; two failure codes with restart semantics; an exact-sequence multi-hop fixture; and per-page work bounds that a replay-earlier-pages design would fail. Deferred items are visible rather than implicit, so a design that cannot meet them must raise pushback against these behaviours instead of quietly diverging. New shared terms `TraversalCursor` and `TraversalPage` enter the division core with evidence traced to the vision and these behaviours.

<a id="entry-docs-architecture-for-traversal-cursor-pagination-122"></a>

## Entry 43 — 2026-11-21 — docs: architecture for traversal cursor pagination (#122)

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The accepted behaviours left the resumption mechanism open (U6): how a breadth-first walk continues exactly-once across a branch boundary without replaying earlier pages, what a cursor binds and in what order it is validated, and how the bounded-work measures (B16/B17) can be met when many neighbours are filtered out. The existing walk discards its frontier at the 100-path cap; inventory and history set a stateless-cursor precedent but have no frontier to carry.

## Decision

[ADR 0019](docs/adr/0019-carry-the-traversal-frontier-in-the-cursor.md): the frontier rides in the cursor as compact edge-reference chains — at most 101 pending expansions at a page boundary, each re-deriving its endpoint, steps, and visited set — resumed mid-node through the neighbour reader's existing keyset position; a per-request examined-step budget (ten times the page size) ends a page early instead of scanning without limit. Server-retained walk state and deterministic replay were considered and rejected (replay is exactly what B16 forbids and measures).

[ADR 0020](docs/adr/0020-bind-traversal-cursors-to-snapshot-and-journal.md): the cursor binds the traversal parameters, the snapshot id, and the workspace journal position; validation runs shape → parameter match → view freshness, so a parameter mismatch reports 422 `invalidCursor` and a moved-on view reports 409 `staleCursor`, through the existing status map with no new codes. Any contribution append invalidates outstanding cursors.

## Consequences

The developer can plan without re-deciding structure: contract additions are additive (`Cursor`/`NextCursor`), the change is confined to Contracts, Store, Api, and their tests, and deployment gains nothing stateful — no tables, migrations, or expiry jobs. The coarse any-edit invalidation is accepted deliberately (cheap, auditable); relaxing it would need a new cursor version and a behaviour change. The PR #117 link conventions extend to the traversal `next` link, and the spec must document both page examples and cursor errors.
